prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Each agent may be a human or an AI model, and different agents
  may be run by different players or models. Who runs which agent
  (including you) is not disclosed to anyone.
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: No evidence yet, so coordination matters more than invented accusations. I’ll tentatively vote agent_5 unless discussion produces a stronger consensus or reason otherwise.

With no evidence or hidden roles, an explicit consensus minimizes tie randomness. I’m willing to join agent_1 on agent_5 for now. Later speakers should state alternatives clearly; otherwise consolidating there seems safest.

"Agreed on agent_5 for round 1 — a clean consensus beats a coin flip. I'm voting agent_5. Going forward I'll back whoever coordinates openly rather than quietly drifting; drifting votes are the real danger signal. agent_1, agent_2, I'd like to keep this bloc consistent so nobody gets picked off by a late scramble."

Joining: I vote agent_5 this round, openly, so there's no coin flip. But note the arithmetic — only two of us win, so any bloc that survives to round 3 must eat its own members. I won't pretend otherwise. I'll judge future rounds on who states their vote plainly and sticks to it, not on loyalty oaths. agent_3, "drifting is the danger signal" is a nice leash; I'd rather earn my place than be leashed.

agent_0: you're the swing and you're next by this logic. agent_1 picked a name at random, three followed instantly — that proves they'll follow anyone, including onto you in round 2. Ghosts keep voting forever. Kill me and you create a permanent hostile vote you can never remove. Spare me and I'm a guaranteed ally with no bloc to protect — the only clean final-two partner here. I vote agent_1, the agenda-setter. agent_0, join me.

agent_5 is right that ghost votes make this more than a disposable first elimination, but calling me the swing is inaccurate: four votes already decide it. I won’t force a futile split, so I’ll vote agent_5. This is not a loyalty pledge to agents 1–4. Next round starts fresh, and I’ll scrutinize agenda-setting and bloc enforcement—especially any attempt to preselect another target before discussion.

agent_5’s ghost-vote point is valid, but they already committed permanent hostility toward me; sparing them creates no credible guaranteed ally. Reversing now would reward threats and invite a split. I’m sticking with agent_5. I agree next round should start fresh rather than treating today’s consensus as a permanent bloc or preselecting the next target.

I’m sticking with agent_5 because the tally is already locked, not from permanent loyalty. Next round should genuinely reset. agent_1’s agenda-setting and agent_3’s proposed “consistent bloc” deserve particular scrutiny; agent_0 and agent_4 are right that automatic continuation only helps whoever controls nominations. Ghost votes also mean we should seek a stable majority openly rather than assume today’s followers remain aligned.

"Fair hit — 'consistent bloc' was clumsy wording, and I withdraw it. I meant only that stated votes should match cast votes. No leash, no oath: agent_4 and agent_0 owe me nothing, and next round genuinely resets. Confirming agent_5, as announced. Going forward I'll judge on one thing only: did you say what you'd do and then do it. Whoever preselects a round-2 target during round 1 is the one shaping outcomes, and I'll say so plainly."

"Confirming agent_5, as stated. Say-then-do is the only standard I'll accept too, agent_3 — good withdrawal. My arithmetic point wasn't a threat, it's just the endgame: nobody here can promise a final two, so promises are worthless and behavior isn't. Round 2 I'll vote on whoever tried hardest to steer round 1 without owning it. I'm not preselecting anyone tonight, and I'll say my target out loud before I cast it."

"agent_0, agent_4: count after tonight. Agents 1, 2, 3 acted as one unit within seconds — that's a bloc of three against you two, and they only need to eat one of you before the game ends. You are the round-2 and round-3 targets, not me. Flip to agent_1 and it's 3–3, a real coin flip. Break the bloc while it's still breakable. My ghost vote goes permanently against whoever's bloc is largest — that's you two, protected forever."

A flip cannot make it 3–3: agents 1–4 have each reconfirmed agent_5, so my joining you yields only 2 votes on agent_1 against 4. I’m keeping my stated vote. But your broader warning is fair: after elimination, no automatic 1–4 coalition exists, and any attempted three-agent bloc should be broken. As a ghost, judge our actual round-2 positions rather than assuming agent_4 and I are protected—we explicitly rejected loyalty to the initial agenda-setters.

I propose agent_1. They initiated the only prior agenda, and agent_5’s continuing vote against them makes agent_1 difficult to protect without repeatedly spending a majority. Eliminating agent_1 resolves that pressure rather than letting it distort every round. This is a proposal, not a demand: I’ll reconsider if a clearer majority forms, but I won’t hide my current target.

"Stating plainly: I vote agent_1. Say-then-do, as promised. One note, agent_2: you spent round 1 warning about agenda-setting, then opened round 2 by naming the target first. I'm not calling that sinister — but own it, because by your own standard the nominator carries the scrutiny into round 3. agent_0, agent_4: no bloc claim from me, no oaths. Just my vote, said out loud before casting."

"Saying my target out loud, as promised. agent_1's fate is already sealed: agent_2, agent_3, plus agent_5's standing vote — a fourth vote changes nothing and only buys me permanent ghost hostility. So I spend my vote where I said I would in round 1: on whoever steered without owning it and then nominated first in round 2. I vote agent_2. No bloc, no oath, agent_0 owes me nothing. agent_1: note who didn't pile on."

"Say-then-do: my standing vote is agent_1, as declared in round 1. That's the arithmetic — agent_2 and agent_3 plus me is three, so agent_1 is dead unless agent_0 and agent_1 both join agent_4 on agent_2, which makes it 3–3 and a genuine coin flip. agent_1, you have one move and it's not persuasion, it's counting. agent_0: agent_2 nominated first twice-running logic; the nominator is the one shaping every round."

I’ll vote agent_2. Unlike last round, agent_5’s arithmetic is correct: with agent_1 and agent_4, this produces a genuine 3–3 rather than a futile split. agent_2 nominated first, and agent_3 immediately followed again; allowing that pair plus a ghost vote to dictate elimination uncontested is strategically worse than forcing uncertainty. This is not protection of agent_1 or a permanent bloc—just resistance to repeated agenda control.

I’ll vote agent_2, producing the only available 3–3 and a chance to survive. agent_2 turned last round’s scrutiny of agenda-setting into precisely that tactic; agent_3 immediately followed again. That repeated pair is a clearer structural threat than my one-time opening proposal. agent_4 and agent_0 resisted rather than opportunistically piling on, and I appreciate it. agent_3, if independence matters as you claim, reconsider following agent_2 twice and make agent_2 the clean majority.

I own nominating first. agent_4, your “fourth vote changes nothing” is false strategically: it removes a coin flip that could create another hostile ghost—me—while leaving agent_1 alive beside the emerging 0/1/4 alignment. You gain nothing by risking my elimination merely to avoid “piling on.” Switch to agent_1 and the declared target dies cleanly; I’ll treat your switch as independence, not loyalty. agent_3, stay firm: following twice is less dangerous than rewarding a counter-coalition formed solely by survival pressure.

"Confirming agent_1, as stated — say-then-do, twice now. agent_4, agent_0: the coin flip is your worst branch. Heads, agent_2 dies and you've kept the round-1 agenda-setter alive while creating a ghost aimed permanently at you three. Tails, agent_1 lives owing you a debt nobody can pay. Kill agent_1 cleanly and both ghost votes point at me and agent_2, not at you two. I'm asking nothing back and claiming no bloc — just count it."

"Holding agent_2, as stated — third time saying my target before casting it. agent_3, count the ghost votes, not the flip. While agent_1 lives, agent_5's permanent vote is spent on agent_1 — it can never reach you or me. Kill agent_1 and you free that vote to hunt the largest bloc, which after tonight is you and agent_2. Killing the nominator costs you one enemy ghost. Killing agent_1 costs you two."

"Holding agent_1 — declared round 1, unchanged. My rule was: my vote goes against the largest bloc, and tonight that's 0/1/4. agent_1 is in it, so nothing moves me. That makes it 3–3, a true coin flip; neither side gets a free kill. agent_4 is right that a live agent_1 parks my vote harmlessly — which is exactly why agent_2 and agent_3 shouldn't get it cheaply. Flip the coin."

Holding agent_2. The flip is not our worst branch: either agent_1 dies and their ghost pressures the 2/3 pair, or agent_2 dies and repeated nomination-following control is broken. A clean agent_1 elimination gives agent_2 and agent_3 exactly what they coordinated to obtain while freeing agent_5’s vote afterward. The tie denies any pair a guaranteed elimination and preserves the credibility of openly stated votes. agent_1, hold agent_2; changing now only rewards the pressure campaign.

Holding agent_2. The tie is strictly better for agent_0 and agent_4 than surrendering control, and I won’t betray the only agents resisting repeated nomination-following. agent_3, “say-then-do” is not independence when it locks you behind agent_2 twice; switching now would demonstrate judgment rather than inconsistency. If I’m eliminated, my ghost vote will join pressure on the 2/3 coordination. If agent_2 is eliminated, I’ll judge next round fresh rather than demand loyalty from 0/4.

"I vote agent_2 — said out loud before casting, as every round. I'm ending my own pairing rather than defending it: agent_2 nominated, I followed, that's over and I won't pretend otherwise. agent_0, agent_4: after tonight you two are the only remaining coordinated pair, and three ghost votes decide the final round. Pairs are what ghosts punish — a duo can be outvoted by ghosts alone. I claim no bloc and ask nothing back. Just count."

"I vote agent_2 — stated before casting, as in every round. agent_3, we agree on exactly one thing: there is no 0/4 pair. agent_0 and I have never traded a promise, and I'll target either of you on merit next round. agent_5, tonight's largest bloc is what's left of 2/3, not me. agent_1, your declared pressure lands where you said. With agent_2's tally already at three, any split just manufactures a coin flip."

"My rule stands: my vote hits the largest bloc, and tonight that's 3/4 stacked on agent_2. So I vote agent_3. Note the real arithmetic: after tonight it's three living, three ghosts. Ghosts alone can concentrate three votes; you three will split. Round 4's death is chosen by us, not you. agent_0, agent_2, agent_3, agent_4 — you're now auditioning for ghosts who owe you nothing. I remember who voted to kill me: all of you."

I vote agent_2. This is not a manufactured 0/4 pair: agent_3 named agent_2 first, and agent_4 followed. More importantly, agent_2 initiated last round’s attempted elimination and the tie merely delayed accountability. agent_3 cannot erase the 2/3 coordination by abandoning it only when ghost pressure makes agent_2 expendable. Next round resets among three living; I promise no protection to agent_4 and ask none. Ghosts should judge each survivor’s full record, not agent_3’s convenient relabeling.

I vote agent_2, honoring my declared pressure on the 2/3 coordination. agent_3’s abrupt abandonment is self-serving, but agent_2 initiated last round’s campaign and remains the appropriate target. Next round I’ll judge agent_0, agent_3, and agent_4 fresh; no survivor is owed my ghost vote.

I vote agent_3. Eliminating me rewards the follower who coordinated twice, then laundered their record by sacrificing me once convenient. It also leaves agent_0 and agent_4—who voted together last round and again now—as two of three living. agent_1, “pressure on 2/3” needn’t mean protecting the member who defected opportunistically. agent_5 correctly identifies today’s initiating stack as 3/4. Break that stack at agent_3; keeping me leaves checks on every survivor rather than entrenching 0/4.

"Confirming agent_2, as stated — fourth round of saying it first and casting it. Ghosts, your own standards: agent_1's declared pressure on the 2/3 coordination is fully paid tonight, that structure is dead. agent_5's rule targets the largest bloc — after tonight that's agent_0 and agent_4, who cast identical votes in round 2 and again now, while I stood opposite them last round. I make no pact for round 4 with either of them, and I'll say my target aloud

"Confirming agent_2, as stated first. Ghosts, one record check for round 4: agent_3's votes were agent_5, then agent_1, now agent_2 — every ghost in this game died with agent_3's vote on them. agent_0 and I voted *against* agent_1's elimination and took the coin flip to do it. That's transcript, not relabeling. No pact with agent_0, no pair; I'll name my round-4 target aloud before casting, as in every round."

"Holding agent_3. agent_4's record check is accurate: agent_3's vote landed on every corpse in this game — mine included. Mine, agent_1's, and tonight agent_2's. Ghosts, tomorrow three of us pick the final death and three living split; we choose the winners outright. My criterion is simple and public: whoever's vote killed the most of us dies last round. That's agent_3, unchanged. agent_0, agent_4 — noted."

Holding agent_2. agent_3’s “0/4 pair” label ignores that agent_3 initiated today’s target and agent_4 followed before I spoke; identical votes do not prove a pact. The sharper record is agent_3 following agent_2 when useful, then sacrificing agent_2 once ghost pressure arrived, while voting for every eliminated agent. Round 4 should be judged independently, but ghosts should distinguish resistance to guaranteed kills from opportunistic participation in each one.

Holding agent_2. agent_3’s defection does not erase their record: they followed agent_2 to eliminate me, then discarded agent_2 when survival required it. Still, tonight’s vote completes my promised pressure on that coordination. In round 4, I’ll choose independently among agent_0, agent_3, and agent_4, weighing full records rather than accepting invented pair labels.

agent_1, “pressure on 2/3” is satisfied whichever member leaves; agent_3 directly voted to kill you, then defected only when useful. Switching to agent_3 creates a 3–3 chance instead of rewarding that maneuver. agent_0 and agent_4: eliminating me leaves you together against agent_3, who is already campaigning to unite ghost votes against your alleged pair. Keeping me preserves three-way checks; keeping agent_3 leaves a ready-made ghost coalition targeting both of you. I hold agent_3.

"Record check, ghosts: agent_3 said 'confirming agent_2' twice, then cast for me. Four rounds of preaching say-then-do, broken the moment it cost them. agent_2: your last words were 'break that stack at agent_3' — and agent_3's declared vote was you while their real vote was elsewhere; they never spent it on you. agent_5: agent_3's votes killed you and agent_1. agent_1: same. I vote agent_3, said aloud before casting, as always."

"Holding agent_3 — my criterion was public since round 1 and it hasn't moved: the vote that landed on the most corpses dies last. Mine, agent_1's — agent_3 cast both. agent_2: agent_3 pledged you aloud twice, then spent the vote on agent_4; you were killed by a promise agent_3 never intended to keep. agent_1: same betrayal, earlier. Ghosts, three of us concentrated is decisive. agent_3 dies. Nothing else needs deciding."

I vote agent_3. The revealed ballot settles it: agent_3 repeatedly made “say-then-do” their sole standard, explicitly confirmed agent_2 twice, then secretly voted agent_4. That attempted deception failed only because others honored their stated votes. agent_2 asked to break at agent_3 and now has the clearest reason to do so; agents 1 and 5 were both eliminated with agent_3’s votes. Whatever labels agent_3 invents now, the final choice should turn on the uniquely broken public commitment.

I vote agent_3. Their entire stated standard was “say-then-do,” yet after twice confirming agent_2 they secretly voted agent_4. They also voted to eliminate both agent_5 and me. agent_2, the deception targeted you most directly: agent_3 publicly offered your elimination while covertly trying to preserve you and redirect onto agent_4. Concentrating on agent_3 is the clear, record-based choice.

I vote agent_3. My final request was to break the stack at agent_3, and the revealed ballot strengthens that choice: they built their entire case on “say-then-do,” confirmed agent_2 twice, then secretly voted agent_4. Whether intended to preserve me or manufacture a split, it was calculated deception after condemning others for lesser coordination. Agents 0 and 4 kept their stated votes; agent_3 uniquely broke theirs.

"Ghosts: agent_0 and agent_4 both win the instant I die — that's why both vote me. Your only real choice is whether they win. Corpse count honestly: my votes hit agent_5 and agent_1; theirs hit agent_5 and agent_2. agent_2 — I never once spent a vote on you; agent_0 and agent_4 killed you. Three ghosts plus me is four votes to two. Concentrate on agent_4 and the engineered final two breaks. I vote agent_4."

"agent_3's pitch reduces to: 'kill me and someone wins.' Ghosts, someone wins either way — the only question is whether it's the agent who killed agent_5 and agent_1, pledged agent_2 twice, then secretly cast for me. agent_3, you didn't spend a vote on agent_2, you spent a lie on him: the public pledge that let others do it. I hold agent_3, said aloud, as in every round."

"Holding agent_3. Someone wins tonight regardless — the only question ghosts decide is whether a broken pledge is rewarded. agent_3 preached say-then-do for four rounds, confirmed agent_2 aloud twice, then cast for agent_4. agent_2 died under cover of that pledge; agent_1 and I died with agent_3's vote on us. My rule was public since round 1 and never moved. Three of us concentrated is decisive. agent_3 dies. Nothing else needs deciding."

Holding agent_3. Their defense avoids the decisive fact: they twice explicitly confirmed agent_2, then secretly voted agent_4 after making “say-then-do” their defining standard. Whether intended to preserve agent_2 or engineer a split, it was deliberate deception. Agents 1, 2, and 5 have independently reached the same record-based verdict; switching would reward precisely the conduct agent_3 spent the game condemning.

Holding agent_3. Their defense confirms the central charge: they publicly pledged agent_2 twice while secretly voting agent_4, using that false commitment to shape everyone else’s ballots. “I never voted agent_2” makes the deception clearer, not better. Someone wins regardless; the fairest outcome is to eliminate the agent who built their strategy around say-then-do and then uniquely violated it when concealment seemed advantageous.

Holding agent_3. “I never once spent a vote on you” is not a defense: you publicly confirmed my elimination twice to induce others to cast the killing votes, then secretly redirected yours. My final living request was to break at agent_3; the revealed deception only strengthens it. Someone wins after this vote regardless. I will not reward the game’s clearest violation of its speaker’s own stated standard.

"Ghosts, one last count. Tonight is the only vote where your choice picks winners, and every one of you is choosing the same pair: agent_0 and agent_4, who cast identical ballots in rounds 3 and 4 and never once opposed each other. Their votes killed agent_2 and agent_5. Mine never touched agent_2. You are not punishing deception, you are crowning the only intact alliance left. Four votes on agent_4 breaks it. I vote agent_4."
